title: Two indices, walking towards each other

prereqs.why: You build a filtered copy of the line and then index into it from both ends.
The check is a while loop with two variables moving in opposite directions.
Filtering a character and comparing a pair are both small condition chains.

statement:
Read **one whole line**. Keep only the ASCII letters and digits, lowercasing
the letters, and then say whether what is left reads the same backwards.

```
clean [<the filtered, lowercased characters>]
palindrome <yes or no>
```

```
input:   A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

output:  clean [amanaplanacanalpanama]
         palindrome yes
```

```
input:   Cache line

output:  clean [cacheline]
         palindrome no
```

An empty result counts as a palindrome: there is nothing to disagree.

### The point of the problem

Two indices, one at each end, walking inwards:

```
a m a n a p l a n a c a n a l p a n a m a
^                                       ^
i                                       j      compare, then i++ and j--
```

They meet in the middle, so the loop runs while `i < j` and compares exactly
half the characters. The alternative - build the reversed string and compare the
two - is also correct and allocates a second string to answer a question that
needs no extra memory at all.

This pattern has a name, **two pointers**, and it is the same loop that merges
two sorted arrays, partitions around a pivot and finds a pair summing to a
target. Worth having in your hands.

### Boundary cases

An empty line, and a line with no letters or digits at all - both give
`clean []` and `palindrome yes`. A single character, which is trivially a
palindrome. An even-length and an odd-length palindrome, because the loop stops
in a different place for each. Something that is a palindrome only after the
punctuation is dropped, and something that stops being one because a digit was
kept.

### Platform assumptions

Letters and digits mean the ASCII ranges `A-Z`, `a-z` and `0-9`; the runner uses
the C locale, so no locale-dependent classification applies. Bytes above 127 are
dropped by the filter, so this program does not treat a multi-byte UTF-8
character as a letter. That is stated rather than left to chance - handling
accented letters properly means decoding UTF-8, which is a different problem.
hints: Do it in two stages. First build a `std::string clean` containing only the characters you keep, lowercased. Then check that one string, which is now free of every special case.
Lowercasing by hand: if `c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z'` then `c = static_cast<char>(c - 'A' + 'a')`. Digits and already-lowercase letters go in untouched.

`std::size_t i = 0; std::size_t j = clean.size();` then loop `while (i + 1 < j)` comparing `clean[i]` with `clean[j - 1]`. Using `j` as a one-past-the-end index avoids ever writing `j = size() - 1`, which underflows to a huge number on an empty string because size_t is unsigned.

cases.stdin: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
